title: But he adds: in bodies. Then he was aware of them bodies before of them coloured
html_source:
If Ulysses is about anything, it is the interaction of our thoughts with others to reveal the self. Stephen is a ‘very short space of time’ from the Tower where he was harangued by the gruff Mulligan. His friend Buck poked fun at him and using the sharpest sword in a bully’s armoury spread bizarre gossip about the most sensitive of topics – ‘the aunt thinks you killed your mother’.

It is no surprise that Stephen decides not to return to Buck Mulligan in the Tower after Buck assumes it’s ok to hold this mirror up to Stephen. You might think it’s ok to stick to your principles and not pray over your mother’s corpse but look at what the community thinks of you !

Why then is Stephen engaging in thought exercises on competing theories of light when he has nowhere to sleep that night ? The truth is we don’t know. The belligerent reader will know the ‘what’ of the introduction to Proteus (Aristotle/Locke/Berkeley) and also the ‘how’ (free association of thought via interior monologue) but no idea why!

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: errrrrrr what.

Sorry, I’ll put it in more direct terms, Ulysses is a series of happenings rather than a series of actions.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Sorry too, my suggestion wasn’t much of a suggestion, and pretty unhelpful. I was just a bit thrown off because this reads as a really interesting and ambitious annotation, but I found it quite difficult to unpack and to get at what its central point was. It seemed to kind of glaze over the actual bit of text under annotation; and the fairly arcane and obfuscated pondering of Aristotle’s and others' theories of light and colour, although you mention them in passing, could have done with a bit more of a direct explanation. And this also mainly discusses Stephen’s thoughts and dealings with Mulligan from the first two chapters, and I’m not sure how this is actually tied to ‘he was aware of them bodies before of them coloured’. There’s no problem with trying to make connections with different parts of the novel, but perhaps it would be a bit more digestible if you explained the ‘theories of light’ at the top, and then how this relates to what has happened between Stephen and Mulligan. For other readers not overly familiar with the novel, the fact that Stephen has decided, at the very end of ‘Telemachus’, not to return that night to the Martello Tower could be pinpointed more exactly, perhaps by an internal hyperlink to this moment (although I see now that nobody has yet annotated this moment).

I am very interested in your assertion that Ulysses is ‘a series of happenings rather than a series of actions’; I would be interested in having that idea mapped a bit more. Do you mean that Ulysses takes place mostly inside the characters' minds (where associations are free, and it’s difficult to pin down why one thought flows into the next), as opposed to orchestrated events that integrate together in an easily discernible plot? Similarly to your point at the top about ‘the interaction of thoughts with others’? (By the way, do you mean ‘with other thoughts’, or with ‘other people’?) Maybe it wouldn’t be a good idea to clog suggestions with fine points of discussion, but I’d like to encourage you to flesh out your observations.
